note: Compares open source and proprietary medical models and the metrics used to judge them.
title: Large language models in healthcare and medical domain: A review

reading.body:
Medical language models show meaningful capability across clinical tasks, but the field lacks consensus on measurement standards and faces unresolved deployment constraints.

The paper surveys LLM applications in healthcare from named entity recognition through question-answering, comparing proprietary and open-source models available to healthcare organizations. It examines performance metrics used to evaluate these systems and identifies technical limitations that persist. The comparison between commercial and open-source options matters for healthcare systems choosing between licensing costs and maintenance burden, though the data shows no clear performance winner emerges from existing evaluation methods.

What the field measures matters more than the measurements themselves. Healthcare organizations deploying these models lack standardized ways to judge whether they work well enough for clinical use, which explains why adoption remains cautious despite demonstrated capability. This measurement gap reflects a broader problem: healthcare LLM evaluation developed ad-hoc across different research groups rather than converging on shared benchmarks.

The review does not directly address compute requirements, infrastructure costs, or power consumption for running these models in healthcare settings. It also does not quantify how much efficiency gains would offset implementation costs or timeline. These omissions matter because healthcare deployment decisions ultimately depend on whether the computational burden and expense align with clinical benefits, questions this survey cannot answer alone.

explain_beginner: The question, taking stock of the whole landscape of large language models being adapted for medicine, from general chatbots to models built specifically on medical text, what can they actually do for healthcare today, and what stands in the way of using them safely. People cared because by 2023 there were dozens of competing models, some general purpose and some purpose built on medical literature, and clinicians and technologists needed one organized picture of what each category was good for and where the real risks sat, rather than reading dozens of separate papers on their own. The review catalogs nine broad use cases, from helping with diagnosis and drafting clinical documentation to analyzing medical literature and interpreting genetic data, and reports that on a standard medical licensing style benchmark, a leading general purpose model scored notably higher than a leading medical specific model, showing that being purpose built for medicine does not automatically mean the best raw performance. What it does not settle, the review synthesizes existing published benchmark numbers and use cases rather than running new original testing, so it inherits whatever gaps existed in the underlying studies, and it does not resolve which specific model a hospital should choose for a given task.
explain_business: A health system deciding between a general purpose model and a medically specialized one now has at least one concrete data point suggesting bigger general purpose models do not automatically lose to specialized medical models on medical benchmarks, so being built specifically for medicine is not by itself a reason to prefer one vendor's model over another. Because several of the top performing proprietary models are not fully open to independent evaluation, buyers often cannot verify a vendor's benchmark claims themselves and must rely on the vendor's own reported numbers, a real due diligence gap worth flagging in any contract. The review's explicit naming of HIPAA, GDPR, and the EU AI Act as unresolved practical challenges signals that legal and compliance review needs to happen before adopting any of these models for real patient data, not as an afterthought once a pilot is already underway. The nine use case taxonomy here is a reasonable starting checklist for a health system to map its own AI ambitions against, from documentation automation to genomics, to see which use cases already have multiple competing tools versus which remain mostly experimental. This is most useful as an orientation document before narrowing to specific vendor evaluation.
explain_practitioner: Method, a narrative survey covering both general purpose large language models, including GPT-3.5, GPT-4, Bard and Gemini, Claude, and Llama, and medically specialized models such as BioBERT, ClinicalBERT, BioGPT, Med-PaLM 2, GatorTron, and BioMistral, organized around nine clinical use cases including diagnosis support, clinical decision support, medical literature analysis, drug discovery, virtual health assistants, radiology and imaging, automated report generation, and genomics. On the MedQA benchmark, GPT-4 is reported to reach 93.06 percent accuracy compared with 83.7 percent for the medically specialized Med-PaLM 2, a meaningful gap favoring the larger general purpose model despite the other model's medical specific training. The review situates these numbers alongside standard general benchmarks like MMLU and HumanEval as well as medical specific ones like MedNLI and PubMedQA, showing performance is evaluated inconsistently across the field rather than on one shared standard. The authors flag real limitations, models function largely as unexplainable black boxes for clinical decision making, training data can embed and then amplify demographic or disease prevalence bias, several of the strongest performing models are not fully publicly available for independent evaluation, and compliance with regulations like HIPAA, GDPR, and the EU AI Act remains a largely unresolved practical challenge for deployment.
